lesson.title: The Strong Past
lesson.subtitle: kom → kwam, zie → zag, geef → gaf — the old vowel dance

hook.title: The Vowel Changes, the Verb Does Not
hook.content: Strong verbs do not take -te or -de; they change their vowel. Kom → kwam, zie → zag, geef → gaf. English does the same in sing/sang/sung; Dutch keeps the pattern in everyday verbs.

pattern.title: One vowel, one tense
pattern.content: Komen → kwam, zien → zag, geven → gaf, nemen → nam, vinden → vond, blijven → bleef. The consonant frame stays; the vowel carries the past.
pattern.linguist_note: Ablaut is the Indo-European vowel gradation behind English sing/sang/sung and Dutch zingen/zong/gezongen.
pattern.trap_note: Do not add -te to a strong verb: koomte and geefde are wrong. The vowel is the tense marker.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (The Strong Past):
exercises.target_answer: komen, zien, geven, nemen, vinden, blijven
exercises.meaning: to come, to see, to give, to take, to find; to think (opinion), to stay
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "The Strong Past": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik kwam gisteren.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “The Strong Past”.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
options: not He gave us a book.
exercises.explanation: “Hij gaf ons een boek.” is word-for-word “He gave us a book.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: One vowel, one tense.

cues: It means: She took the train.

exercises.affirmation: You heard “Zij nam de trein.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising One vowel, one tense.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I stayed home.”
twist.explanation: Blijven changes its vowel to bleef; no dental ending appears.

summary.outcome: Recognise and use the highest-frequency strong past forms.
summary.takeaway: Some pasts are vowel changes, not suffixes; English and Dutch share the habit.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Strong Verb Gym.

komen.etymology_derivation: English come and Dutch komen are the same verb; the vowel differs.

zien.etymology_derivation: English see and Dutch zien are the same verb; Dutch lost the h.

geven.etymology_derivation: English give and Dutch geven are the same verb; English g comes from Norse influence.

nemen.etymology_derivation: English nim is archaic; Dutch nemen kept the everyday verb.

vinden.etymology_derivation: English find and Dutch vinden are the same verb; Dutch also uses it for opinions.

blijven.etymology_derivation: English stay is a different verb; Dutch blijven is the direct Germanic twin of German bleiben.
